```{r}
source("R/clt_helpers.R")
```

## 1. The population
```{r}
set.seed(student_id)
x <- sample(1:6, 10000, replace = TRUE)

hist(x, breaks = seq(0.5, 6.5, by = 1), probability = TRUE,
     col = "skyblue", border = "white",
     main = "Population: Individual Die Rolls",
     xlab = "Value", ylim = c(0, 0.25))
abline(h = 1/6, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
data.frame(
  quantity  = c("Mean", "SD", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis"),
  theory    = c(3.5, sqrt(35/12), 0, -222/175),
  simulated = round(c(mean(x), sd(x), skew(x), kurt(x)), 3)
)
```

The die population is discrete and uniform: each of the values 1 to 6 has probability 1/6. It is perfectly symmetric about its mean of 3.5, so its skewness is 0, and it is bounded, with no values beyond 1 and 6, so it has no tails at all. Its excess kurtosis is -222/175 = -1.269, negative because a flat distribution has lighter tails than a normal. The standard deviation is sqrt(35/12) = 1.708. The simulated values from 10,000 rolls agree closely. This population never changes during the experiment. Only the distribution of the sample means changes as n grows.

## 2. Prediction
The die is symmetric, so the skewness of the sample mean should be about 0 at every n. Its population excess kurtosis is -222/175 = -1.269, so the excess kurtosis of the mean is -1.269 / n. Requiring |kurtosis| < 0.3 gives n > 4.23, so I predict kurtosis first passes at n = 5 (predicted -0.254), though that is close to the cutoff and simulation noise (about +/-0.022) could affect it. The standard error criterion should hold at every n. Kurtosis, not skewness, is therefore the numeric criterion I expect to decide the answer. I expect the Q-Q plot to show steps at small n, because the sample means can only take values on a grid of multiples of 1/n.

## 3. My criterion
I decided on these criteria before running any simulations (see the README).
A sampling distribution of the mean is "approximately normal" when ALL of
the following hold:

1. |skewness| < 0.2
2. |excess kurtosis| < 0.3
3. The normal Q-Q plot follows the line across the central region with no systematic curve. Small random departures at the extreme tails are acceptable.
4. The simulated SD of the sample means is within 2% of the theoretical   standard error, sigma / sqrt(n) (ratio between 0.98 and 1.02).

I report the smallest tested n at which this and every larger tested n pass all four criteria.

## 4. Simulation
I simulated B = 50,000 sample means at each of 12 sample sizes. I used the same grid and the same B as for the exponential so the populations can be compared directly. The grid includes n = 30 to test the common rule of thumb.

```{r}
ns  <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, 300)
res <- run_clt(function(n) sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE), ns,
               mu = 3.5, sigma = sqrt(35/12), B = 50000)
```

## 5. Evidence
### Numerical table
```{r}
tab <- add_checks(res$table)
knitr::kable(
  tab[, c("n", "skew", "excess_kurt", "sd_ratio",
          "skew_ok", "kurt_ok", "se_ok", "all_numeric")],
  digits = 3
)
```

```{r}
smallest_n(tab)
```
By the numeric criteria, the smallest tested n at which this and every larger tested n pass is 5. The n = 2 row fails only the kurtosis criterion (-0.65, as predicted by -1.269 / 2); every row from n = 5 up passes all three numeric criteria.

### Histograms with the normal curve
```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
for (n in c(2, 5, 10, 30)) {
  plot_clt(res$means[[as.character(n)]], n, mu = 3.5, sigma = sqrt(35/12))
}
```

### Q-Q plots
- n = 5: The sample means fall on a grid of multiples of 0.2, so the plot is a staircase and the histogram shows gaps (a binning artifact, not non-normality). The steps follow the line through the middle. The extreme ends curl slightly inward (light tails), which fits the negative excess kurtosis (-0.24). I judge this a pass, though a mild one.
- n = 10: The steps follow the line with no bow through the middle. The inward curl at the extremes is weaker than at n = 5, as predicted. Pass.
- n = 30: (describe what you see)

## 6. Comparison with theory

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  tab[, c("n", "sim_mean", "theory_mean", "sim_sd", "theory_se", "sd_ratio")],
  digits = 4
)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot(tab$n, tab$sd_ratio, type = "b", pch = 16, log = "x",
     ylim = c(0.95, 1.05), xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)",
     ylab = "Simulated SD / theoretical SE",
     main = "Die: standard error check")
abline(h = 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(h = c(0.98, 1.02), col = "gray50", lty = 2)
```
The simulated means agree with the theoretical mean of 3.5 at every sample size, and the simulated SD of the means agrees with sqrt(35/12) / sqrt(n) within about 0.4% at every n (ratios between 0.996 and 1.003). As with the other populations, the center and spread match theory even at n = 2, where the shape is still not normal.

## 7. Conclusion
**Smallest tested n at which the sampling distribution is approximately normal (all four criteria): n = 5.**

| Criterion             | First passes at | Notes                                             |
|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Skewness < 0.2        | all tested n    | Symmetric population, skewness about 0 at every n |
| Excess kurtosis < 0.3 | between 2 and 5 | Theory: 1.269/n < 0.3 gives n > 4.23              |
| SD within 2% of SE    | all tested n    |                                                   |
| Q-Q plot (visual)     | n = 5 (mild)    | Steps follow the line; ends curl slightly inward  |
| **All four**          | **5**           | Kurtosis decides the answer                      |

The die fails only at n = 2, where the mean of two dice has a triangular shape with lighter tails than a normal (excess kurtosis -0.65). By n = 5 the kurtosis is -0.24, inside my cutoff by only about 0.06, so the pass at n = 5 is close to the edge. My grid has no n = 3 or n = 4, so I can only say the kurtosis crossing lies between 2 and 5 (theory puts it at n = 4.23). By this evidence n = 30 is more than enough for a die.

## 8. Surprises and limitations
- The sample means of a discrete population sit on a grid (multiples of 1/n), so the histograms show gaps and spikes at small n and the Q-Q plots are staircases. At n = 5 the histogram bars were about twice as tall as the normal curve because the bins were narrower than the grid spacing. That is a plotting artifact, so I judged shape from the Q-Q plot and the numerical summaries instead.
- Kurtosis, not skewness, decided the numeric answer. This is the opposite of the exponential, because the die is symmetric but has light tails.
- Light tails produce an inward curl at the ends of the Q-Q plot, the opposite direction from the exponential's outward drift.
- The kurtosis at n = 5 (-0.24) is close to my cutoff of 0.3, and the simulation noise is about +/-0.022, so this pass is not by a wide margin.
- My grid skips n = 3 and 4, so the crossing is only located between 2 and 5.
